about: The roster of At the table: every style, in the Cask Atlas (Whisky & Brandy, key casks), 5 November 2026: the thirty-four whisky styles a guest may name, each with a professional tableside presentation on the liquor shelf's pattern. A row carries its id (frozen once keys.v1.json is frozen: a card key is a person's record), the name the page prints, its family (american, scotch, irish, japanese, canadian, drawn in that order), its authoring chunk, terms (the words that name the style: s10, s45 and the recall prompt carry one as a whole phrase, and the page's search reads them), neighbour (the style its compare field sets it against, drawn as a link), chapters (Cask Atlas chapter ids, CASK_CHAPTERS in js/data-casks.js, the first the chapter it belongs to), shelf (liquor shelf bottle ids, BACKBAR_GUIDE in js/data-backbar.js: the bottles a guest would hear presented as this style; O.F.C. stands under bourbon and straight whiskey, and every American whiskey on the shelf stands under at least one style), canon (COCKTAILS slugs in js/data-core.js through the app's slugify: the classics the style belongs in, the first the one serve.classic names first) and, where one helps, a note for the author: a fact to verify against the rule itself, never text for the page. Authors read this file; schema.mjs and build-caskstyles.mjs hold the fragments to it. A fragment copies family, shelf, chapters and canon from its row; an author who finds a better link changes the row and the fragment together.

chunks.s1: bourbon (the federal standard); wheated bourbon; high-rye bourbon; four-grain and multigrain bourbon; straight whiskey
chunks.s2: bottled-in-bond; small batch and single barrel; barrel proof (cask strength); Tennessee whiskey (the Lincoln County Process and the 2013 law); Kentucky-style rye; Maryland and Pennsylvania (Monongahela) rye
chunks.s3: American single malt (the 2024 standard); corn whiskey; wheat whiskey; blended American and light whiskey; Canadian whisky
chunks.s4: Scotch single malt; single grain Scotch; blended malt; blended Scotch; Speyside
chunks.s5: the Highlands; the Islands (a part of the Highlands in law); the Lowlands; Islay; Campbeltown
chunks.s6: Irish single pot still; Irish single malt; Irish single grain; blended Irish whiskey (triple distillation where it applies)
chunks.s7: Japanese whisky and its 2021 standard and 2025 logo; Japanese single malt; Japanese blended whisky and the highball; Mizunara oak

entries.name: Bourbon
entries.note: 27 CFR 5.143(c)(2): produced in the United States at no more than 80% ABV from a mash of at least 51 per cent corn, stored at no more than 62.5% ABV in charred new oak, bottled at 40% ABV or more, no added colouring, flavouring or blending materials. No minimum age for bourbon itself; Kentucky is not required (the 1964 resolution of Congress named it a distinctive product of the United States).

entries.name: Wheated bourbon
entries.note: No legal category of its own: bourbon with wheat, not rye, as the second grain. Wheat is often found softer and rounder; the grain is one influence among yeast, barrel, proof and age (PLAN.md B, the line the bourbon chapter and the Weller bottles share).

entries.name: High-rye bourbon
entries.note: No legal threshold for high rye: a trade term for a bourbon whose rye share is well above the usual, often given as around 20 to 35 per cent. Say so; quote a producer's own published recipe only.

entries.name: Four-grain and multigrain bourbon
entries.note: No legal category: bourbon (at least 51 per cent corn) with both rye and wheat beside the malted barley, or with further grains. Rabbit Hole Cavehill's own recipe is corn, malted wheat, malted barley and honey malted barley (its fragment): a four-grain recipe built without rye.

entries.name: Straight whiskey
entries.note: 27 CFR 5.143: at least two years in charred new oak for the straight types, no added colouring, flavouring or blending materials; an age statement is required under four years; a mix of straight whiskies of the same type made in one state stays straight (the same-state rule, PLAN.md B).

entries.name: Bottled-in-bond
entries.note: The Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897, now 27 CFR 5.88: one distilling season, one distiller at one distillery, at least four years in a bonded warehouse under government supervision, bottled at exactly 100 proof, the distillery named on the label.

entries.name: Small batch and single barrel
entries.note: Neither term is defined in federal law: small batch is the producer's own word for a smaller mingling of barrels; single barrel means one cask, bottled alone. Say what the label promises and no more.

entries.name: Barrel proof
entries.note: TTB labelling policy (the Beverage Alcohol Manual): barrel proof and cask strength describe whisky bottled at about the strength it came out of the barrel, entry proof or original proof the strength it went in; verify the exact tolerance from TTB before stating it. Never give one batch's proof as the style's.

entries.name: Tennessee whiskey
entries.note: The 2013 Tennessee law (Tennessee Code 57-2-106), cited as the law: made in Tennessee from at least 51 per cent corn, filtered through maple charcoal before ageing (the Lincoln County Process), aged in new charred oak, at least 40% ABV, with its exception for Benjamin Prichard's in Lincoln County (PLAN.md B).

entries.name: Kentucky-style rye
entries.note: Not a legal category: a trade name for a rye made on a bourbon frame, just over the 51 per cent rye line with plenty of corn, as against the rye-heavy Maryland and Pennsylvania tradition. Rye whisky is 27 CFR 5.143 (at least 51 per cent rye, charred new oak).

entries.name: Maryland and Monongahela rye
entries.note: Historic regional styles, not legal categories: Monongahela, the rye of western Pennsylvania, usually described as rye-heavy with little or no corn, and Maryland rye, often described as softer and sweeter. Only what two sources agree on; nothing about a present producer's stock.

entries.name: American single malt
entries.note: TTB's standard of identity was published on 18 December 2024 and took effect on 19 January 2025: 100 per cent malted barley, mashed, distilled and matured in the United States, distilled at one distillery, at no more than 80% ABV, in oak casks of no more than 700 litres, bottled at 40% ABV or more (PLAN.md B). Never the 2025 standard.

entries.name: Corn whiskey
entries.note: 27 CFR 5.143: at least 80 per cent corn, at no more than 80% ABV; if stored, in used or uncharred new oak at no more than 62.5% ABV; never treated with charred wood. Straight corn whiskey has at least two years.

entries.name: Wheat whiskey
entries.note: 27 CFR 5.143: at least 51 per cent wheat, at no more than 80% ABV, stored at no more than 62.5% ABV in charred new oak. Not wheated bourbon, which is at least 51 per cent corn.

entries.name: Blended American and light whiskey
entries.note: 27 CFR 5.143: blended whisky holds at least 20 per cent straight whisky by proof gallons, the rest whisky or neutral spirits; light whiskey is distilled above 80% and below 95% ABV and stored in used or uncharred new oak.

entries.name: Single malt Scotch
entries.note: The Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009: distilled at one distillery from water and malted barley only, in pot stills, then the Scotch rules (matured in Scotland at least three years in oak casks of no more than 700 litres, at least 40% ABV, only water and plain caramel added).

entries.name: Single grain Scotch
entries.note: The Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009: distilled at one distillery, from malted barley with or without other malted or unmalted cereals, and not a single malt; usually in column stills, though the rule names no still.

entries.name: Blended malt Scotch
entries.note: The Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009: single malts from more than one distillery, no grain whisky. The older words vatted malt and pure malt are no longer allowed on a label; verify the date.

entries.name: Blended Scotch
entries.note: The Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009: one or more single malts blended with one or more single grains. Nothing about which share of malt a brand uses unless the producer publishes it.

entries.name: Speyside
entries.note: A protected region under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009, inside the Highland area; a name on the label means the whisky was wholly distilled there. Region is evidence of geography, not proof of flavour (the chapter's own line).

entries.name: Highland
entries.note: A protected region under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009; the Islands other than Islay fall inside it in law. A name on the label means the whisky was wholly distilled in the region.

entries.name: The Islands
entries.note: Not a protected region: an informal grouping (Orkney, Skye, Mull, Jura, Arran, Lewis, Raasay and others) whose whiskies are Highland in law (the chapter's own fact). Islay is apart, a protected locality.

entries.name: Lowland
entries.note: A protected region under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009. Triple distillation is a tradition at some Lowland distilleries, never the rule; say which house does it.

entries.name: Islay
entries.note: A protected locality under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009, with Campbeltown. The name means wholly distilled on Islay; the law asks nothing about peat, and some of the island's distilleries make unpeated malt.

entries.name: Campbeltown
entries.note: A protected locality under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009, defined in the regulation by the South Kintyre ward. Name its working distilleries only from two sources; nothing about who owns them.

entries.name: Irish single pot still
entries.note: The Irish whiskey technical file: a mash of at least 30 per cent malted and at least 30 per cent unmalted barley, up to 5 per cent other unmalted cereals, distilled in copper pot stills (double or triple), at least three years in wood on the island of Ireland. The 2026 consultation on raising other cereals to 30 per cent is a proposal, never the rule (PLAN.md B).

entries.name: Irish single malt
entries.note: The Irish whiskey technical file: 100 per cent malted barley, distilled in pot stills at one distillery, at least three years in wood on the island of Ireland. Peated or not, double or triple distilled: the house's choice.

entries.name: Irish single grain
entries.note: The Irish whiskey technical file: column distilled from a mash with no more than 30 per cent malted barley and other cereals such as maize, wheat or barley, at one distillery for single. The 2026 consultation's grain proposal is a proposal only.

entries.name: Blended Irish whiskey
entries.note: The Irish whiskey technical file: a blend of two or more of malt, pot still and grain Irish whiskey. Triple distillation is common, never required.

entries.name: Japanese whisky
entries.note: The Japan Spirits & Liqueurs Makers Association standard (2021; existing products had until 31 March 2024) is an association standard, not a law: malted grain always used, mashed, fermented and distilled in Japan with water drawn in Japan, at least three years in wood of no more than 700 litres in Japan, bottled in Japan at 40% ABV or more. The association's 2025 logo and its push towards a binding rule: state each as what it is (PLAN.md B).

entries.name: Japanese single malt
entries.note: Malted barley at one distillery; under the association standard it must also meet the Japanese whisky chain. Name historic houses and their founding dates only from two sources.

entries.name: Japanese blended whisky and the highball
entries.note: Malt and grain whiskies blended; the highball (whisky and chilled soda, built cold) is the serve the style is known by at home. Teach the build, not a brand's measure.

entries.name: Mizunara oak
entries.note: Quercus mongolica (crispula), Japanese oak: porous, slow-growing and hard to make tight casks from; used mostly for finishing or a share of a vatting. A cask, not a category: the label word promises some time in that wood and no more. Poured neat, so no classic.

entries.name: Canadian whisky
entries.note: The Food and Drug Regulations B.02.020: mashed, distilled and aged in Canada, at least three years in small wood of no more than 700 litres, at least 40% ABV; caramel and flavouring may be added. Canadian rye whisky names no minimum rye share (the chapter's own fact).
